entities.name: Global & Multi-Regional
entities.summary: Everything that is not one region: worldwide frames and events, and the spans that cross regional boundaries.
entities.date_note: Renamed from 'Global'. The old summary read 'cross-regional and worldwide frames', which ran together two different claims -- being everywhere, and being in several places at once. Empires that span regions are filed in the region they came from and cross-linked to the others; each entity's `regions` list records every region it touches.

name_forms.name: Global
name_forms.note: The earlier name, which invited world events and multi-region empires into the same bucket.

entities.name: Europe
entities.summary: From the Aegean Bronze Age through the modern EU. Split into Mediterranean, Western, Central, Northern, and Eastern sub-branches.

entities.name: Mediterranean
entities.summary: The Greek, Roman and Byzantine worlds and the sea that connected them, treated as one region because its societies were more closely linked to each other by water than to their own inland neighbours.

entities.name: Western Europe
entities.summary: Iberia, France, the Low Countries and the British Isles, from the post-Roman kingdoms through the Atlantic empires.

entities.name: Central Europe
entities.summary: The German-speaking lands, the Alps and the Carpathian basin: the Holy Roman Empire and the Habsburg and Prussian states that succeeded it.

entities.name: Northern Europe
entities.summary: Scandinavia, the Baltic and Finland, including the Norse expansion that reached Greenland and North America.

entities.name: Eastern Europe
entities.summary: The lands between the Baltic and the Black Sea: Kievan Rus', Poland-Lithuania, Muscovy and the Russian states that grew from them. The boundary with Central Europe is political and has moved repeatedly.

entities.name: West Asia
entities.summary: Mesopotamia, the Levant, Anatolia, Iran, and Arabia.

name_forms.name: Middle East
name_forms.note: Coined by the naval strategist Mahan in 1902 for a buffer zone guarding the route to India. Measured from London.

name_forms.name: Near East
name_forms.note: The older British term for the Ottoman lands, 'near' relative to Europe and now largely superseded outside archaeology.

name_forms.name: West Asia
name_forms.note: The geographic term, and the one this dataset uses: it locates the region on its own continent rather than by distance from London.

caveats.text: 'Near' and 'Middle' East are measured from Europe. This dataset files the region as West Asia for that reason, which is itself a choice rather than a neutral default.

entities.name: Mesopotamia & Levant
entities.summary: The Tigris-Euphrates floodplain and the Levantine coast, where writing, cities and law codes first appear in the record.

entities.name: Anatolia
entities.summary: The peninsula between the Aegean and the Caucasus: Hittite, Phrygian, Lydian, Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Turkish in succession.

entities.name: Iran

name_forms.name: Iran
name_forms.note: Always the internal name. The 1935 change was to what foreigners were asked to say, not to what Iranians called their country.

name_forms.name: Persia
name_forms.note: The Greek-derived exonym Europe used. Foreign governments were asked to drop it with effect from 21 March 1935.

caveats.text: Persia was never the country's own name. Iran is the endonym, and in 1934 the government gave foreign states three months' notice to start using it.

entities.summary: The Iranian plateau and its empires, from Elam and the Achaemenids to the Safavids and the modern state.

entities.name: Arabia
entities.summary: The peninsula and its incense kingdoms before Islam, and the states that followed.

entities.name: Central Asia & the Steppe
entities.summary: Silk Road oases, the Eurasian steppe, and Tibet.

name_forms.name: Inner Asia
name_forms.note: Overlapping rather than synonymous: Inner Asia usually reaches further into Mongolia and Manchuria.

name_forms.name: Turkestan
name_forms.note: The 19th-century Russian and British name for the region, divided into Russian and Chinese halves.

entities.name: Central Asia
entities.summary: The oasis cities and river valleys of Transoxiana and Khorasan — Samarkand, Bukhara, Merv — repeatedly the hinge between the settled empires around them.

entities.name: Eurasian Steppe
entities.summary: The grassland corridor from Mongolia to Hungary, and the mobile polities that formed across it. Their borders were seasonal and their records are usually written by their neighbours.

entities.name: Tibet & Himalaya
entities.summary: The plateau and the Himalaya: the Tibetan Empire that once rivalled Tang China, and the Buddhist polity that followed it.

entities.name: South Asia
entities.summary: Indian subcontinent from Indus civilization through the modern republics.

name_forms.name: Indian subcontinent
name_forms.note: Geographic rather than political, and older than the states in it.

entities.name: East Asia
entities.summary: China, Korea and Japan, plus the steppe and maritime peripheries they contested, linked by a shared script, canon and diplomatic order.

entities.name: China
entities.summary: The longest continuously documented state tradition on record, from the Neolithic cultures of the Yellow and Yangtze valleys to the present. Dynastic names organise it, but they conceal as much as they reveal: several were regional, several overlapped, and some conquered from outside.

entities.name: Korea
entities.summary: The peninsula from Gojoseon and the Three Kingdoms through Silla, Goryeo and Joseon to the modern division.

entities.name: Japan
entities.summary: The archipelago from Jōmon foraging societies through the imperial court, the shogunates and the modern state. Its eras are named reign periods, which is why so many appear here.

entities.name: Southeast Asia
entities.summary: The mainland peninsulas and the island world between India and China. The name is a twentieth-century military coinage; the region's own states organised themselves around river valleys and sea lanes, not around this category.

entities.name: Mainland Southeast Asia
entities.summary: The Irrawaddy, Chao Phraya, Mekong and Red River valleys: the Burmese, Thai, Lao, Khmer, Cham and Vietnamese states.

entities.name: Maritime Southeast Asia

name_forms.name: East Indies
name_forms.note: The European trading name, and the reason the Caribbean ended up called the West Indies.

entities.summary: The archipelagos and straits — Srivijaya, Majapahit, the sultanates, the Philippine polities — where control meant control of shipping rather than of territory.

entities.name: Africa
entities.summary: The continent where the human lineage originates, and the states, trade systems and empires that followed across a landmass big enough to hold several unconnected histories at once.

entities.name: Nile Valley & Northeast Africa
entities.summary: The Nile corridor and the Horn: Egypt, Nubia and Kush, Aksum and Ethiopia — societies shaped by a river that floods on schedule.

entities.name: North Africa

name_forms.name: Maghreb
name_forms.note: Arabic for 'the west'. Usually the western part rather than the whole of North Africa, so the two are not quite synonyms.

name_forms.name: Barbary Coast
name_forms.note: An early modern European name for the coast, now avoided.

entities.summary: The Maghreb and the Mediterranean littoral: Carthage, Roman Africa, the Berber dynasties and the Islamic states.

entities.name: West Africa & Sahel
entities.summary: The Sahel and the forest belt, where Ghana, Mali, Songhai, Kanem-Bornu and Benin grew on the trade crossing the Sahara.

entities.name: East Africa
entities.summary: The Swahili coast and the interlacustrine kingdoms, connected by monsoon trade to Arabia, India and China.

entities.name: Central Africa
entities.summary: The Congo basin and its forests, where the Kingdom of Kongo and the Luba and Lunda states formed. Thinly represented here relative to its importance, which is a gap in this dataset rather than in the history.

entities.name: Southern Africa
entities.summary: From Great Zimbabwe and Mapungubwe to the Mutapa state and the Zulu kingdom.

entities.name: Americas
entities.summary: Two continents settled from Asia in the late Pleistocene, whose societies developed in near-total isolation from Afro-Eurasia until 1492 — which makes their parallels with it, agriculture and cities and states, the most useful controlled comparison in human history.

entities.name: North America
entities.summary: North of Mesoamerica: the Ancestral Puebloan and Mississippian societies, the Arctic and subarctic peoples, and the nations encountered and displaced by European settlement.

entities.name: Mesoamerica
entities.summary: From central Mexico to Honduras: Olmec, Zapotec, Maya, Teotihuacan, Toltec, Purépecha and Aztec, sharing a calendar, a ballgame and a writing tradition.

entities.name: Intermediate Area & Caribbean
entities.summary: The isthmus and the Caribbean, between the Mesoamerican and Andean worlds and connected to both.

entities.name: Andes
entities.summary: The Pacific coast and highlands from Norte Chico through Moche, Nazca and Wari to the Inca — states built without the wheel, the arch or a writing system as usually defined.

entities.name: Amazon & Southern Cone
entities.summary: Amazonia and the southern cone, including the earthworks and managed forests that overturned the idea of the basin as untouched wilderness.

entities.name: Oceania
entities.summary: Australia, New Guinea and the Pacific islands: the longest continuous cultural traditions known, alongside the last major human migration, which settled the remotest islands on Earth by deliberate open-ocean voyaging.

entities.name: Australia
entities.summary: The continent held by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples for tens of thousands of years before British colonisation.

entities.name: Melanesia
entities.summary: New Guinea and the islands east of it, among the most linguistically diverse places on Earth and an independent centre of agricultural origin.

entities.name: Micronesia
entities.summary: The small islands of the western Pacific, including the megalithic city of Nan Madol built on artificial islets.

entities.name: Polynesia
entities.summary: The triangle from Hawaii to New Zealand to Rapa Nui, settled by navigators who crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean and, in several cases, returned.

entities.name: Paleolithic
entities.summary: The long first chapter: stone tools, fire, and hunter-gatherer life, from the earliest knapped stone through the whole span of the genus Homo.
entities.date_note: Starts at the earliest known stone tools — Lomekwi 3, c. 3.3 Ma — which predate the genus Homo. Whether those count as Oldowan is a definitional argument; they are included here because the toolmaking record is continuous even where the taxonomy is not. name_forms.name: Old Stone Age
name_forms.note: The English calque of the Greek. Part of the three-age scheme whose worldwide application is contested on this entity's parent.

entities.name: Mesolithic (Eurasia)
entities.date_note: The span here is the conventional European one and should not be read as global. Africa uses Later Stone Age, introduced by Goodwin and Van Riet Lowe in 1929; the Americas use Archaic; Southwest Asia uses Epipalaeolithic. The cultures usually meant by the word — Maglemose, Kongemose, Ertebolle, the Azilian, the Sauveterrian — sit under European prehistory in this dataset, because that is where the term has content. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A European period name that much of the world does not use, and a live argument about whether it describes a real stage at all.

caveats.text: Czarnik argued the Mesolithic began as a negative category, defined by being neither Palaeolithic nor Neolithic. Braidwood called the whole tripartite scheme artificial.
There is no universal package of microliths, forest adaptation and coastal sedentism. South Asian microliths appear from about 45,000 years ago, long before any Mesolithic stage.
Elliott and Warren argue exporting the term pegs the rest of the world to a northern European developmental stage. They keep using it for Europe, where it still earns its place.

entities.name: Bronze Age
entities.date_note: Regional Bronze Ages began at different dates; the collapse cluster is c. 1200-1150 BCE. Thomsen devised the Stone/Bronze/Iron scheme in 1837 to order northern European material. Connah's verdict on exporting it: applying it to African archaeology 'produced little more than confusion, whereas in the Americas or Australasia it has been irrelevant'.

caveats.text: A northern European scheme applied worldwide. It has little utility for sub-Saharan Africa, much of Asia and the Americas, where specialists largely do not use it.
The clean 3300 BC seam with the Neolithic hides a regionally variable Copper Age; see the regional Chalcolithic entries.

entities.summary: Age of bronze metallurgy, ending in the systemic Late Bronze Age Collapse c. 1200 BCE.

entities.name: Legendary Age (Three Sovereigns & Five Emperors)
entities.summary: The sage-rulers of Chinese tradition, placed before the Xia: god-kings credited with agriculture, medicine, writing and silk, then five emperors held up for millennia as the model of virtuous rule.
entities.date_note: Traditional bounds, not findings. The tradition has no single canonical form — five different lists of the Three Sovereigns appear in Han-dynasty classics, and the Five Emperors have as many competing groupings. Fuxi and Shennong appear in every list of Sovereigns and are authored beneath; the third slot is variously Suiren, Nüwa, Zhurong, Gonggong or the Yellow Emperor, so it is described here rather than filled by picking one list.

caveats.text: These are mythological figures. The tradition is real and consequential; the rulers are not attested archaeologically.
The regnal dates were calculated by 17th-century Jesuits from Chinese chronicles, then adopted in China via Sun Yat-sen and the 1938 Cihai.

entities.name: Neolithic Transition
entities.summary: Independent, and largely unconscious, transitions to farming in at least seven regions. A process of millennia, not an event.
entities.date_note: NOT A REVOLUTION, despite the name it is still filed under. The dominant model is protracted and geographically autonomous: domestication took on the order of 4,000 years, happened independently at several foci, and was largely unconscious rather than invented. The field has largely replaced Childe's 'Neolithic Revolution' with 'Neolithic transition' for that reason. The end date is diachronous and runs past the Neolithic label itself, because Eastern North America domesticates thousands of years after the Fertile Crescent. alternatives.label: Rapid, conscious, core-area domestication
alternatives.note: Abbo and Gopher argue for a fast deliberate process in one core area.

caveats.text: Not a revolution and not an event: the transition took millennia, and foraging and farming coexisted throughout much of it.
How many independent centres exist is unsettled: Harlan counted 6, Vavilov 12, Purugganan and Fuller 24.
Called a Transition here rather than a Revolution: the process took roughly four thousand years in Southwest Asia, which is not what the word revolution conveys.

entities.name: Human Prehistory
entities.summary: From the earliest stone toolmaking to the first written records. Dated by measurement rather than reckoning, so quoted in years before present.
entities.date_note: SCOPE GATE. This app begins where human-like BEHAVIOUR begins, not where a taxon does. The floor is the earliest knapped stone — currently Lomekwi 3 at 3.3 Ma, which predates the oldest Homo fossil by about 500,000 years. A taxonomic floor would exclude the oldest instance of the very behaviour this app exists to track, and taxonomy is the least stable line available: H. habilis placement is disputed and the Ledi-Geraru mandible is unnamed. Knapping is the line rather than tool use, because tool use extends to chimpanzees and orangutans and so runs past the ~7 Ma common ancestor, which would make any floor arbitrary. The end is diachronous: writing appears at different times in different regions. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: The floor is a behaviour, not a site. If an older knapping site is accepted, this date moves and the app's scope does not change.

entities.date_note: Skeletal remains to about 60 ka, associated artefacts from about 190 ka and continuing to about 50 ka. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Original 2004 chronology
alternatives.note: Withdrawn in 2016: the dated deposits proved to be a younger unit unconformably overlying the remains.

caveats.text: Often reported as surviving until 12,000 years ago. That date was corrected to around 60,000 in 2016.

entities.summary: A small-bodied human on the Indonesian island of Flores, known from Liang Bua cave.

entities.name: Homo luzonensis
entities.date_note: Minimum age revised upward to at least 134 ka in 2023. No youngest-remains date is established; the original 67 ka metatarsal age is now read as a minimum from the dating method rather than a true age. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A human species known from a handful of bones and teeth in a cave on Luzon, the Philippines.

entities.name: Homo sapiens
entities.date_note: 315 +/- 34 ka is the thermoluminescence age of heated flints with the Jebel Irhoud hominins in Morocco. Which fossils count as H. sapiens is itself part of the disagreement about the date.
entities.summary: Our own species, first recognisable in Africa around 300,000 years ago.

entities.name: Homo longi
entities.date_note: Known from one cranium with a minimum U-series age of about 146 ka, so there is no species-level range. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Harbin cranium is Denisovan
alternatives.note: Palaeoproteomic analysis in 2025 recovered 95 endogenous proteins and clustered the specimen with Denisova 3.

caveats.text: Named as a new species in 2021; 2025 protein evidence indicates the specimen is a Denisovan.

entities.summary: A single large skull from Harbin, China, whose identity was overturned by protein analysis in 2025.

name_forms.name: Homo longi
name_forms.note: 'Dragon' for Heilongjiang, the Black Dragon River province.

name_forms.name: Harbin cranium
name_forms.note: The specimen name, preferred by those who doubt the species is distinct.

entities.name: Oldowan Industry
entities.date_note: Usually given as 2.6-1.7 Ma. Older claims exist, but the 3.3 Ma Lomekwi 3 tools are excluded by classifying them as Lomekwian, so the boundary is definitional as much as evidential. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The earliest widely recognised stone tools: sharp flakes struck from pebble cores.

entities.name: Acheulean Industry
entities.date_note: Earliest at Kokiselei 4, West Turkana, Kenya, at 1.76 Ma — about 350,000 years earlier than previously accepted. The end is diffuse rather than dated. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The handaxe tradition: teardrop-shaped tools worked on both faces, made for well over a million years.

entities.name: Mousterian Industry
entities.date_note: Hard to separate from the latest Acheulean at the start, so the beginning is definitional and no single method fixes it. The end differs by region and by method, and is radiocarbon where it can be reached. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. entities.summary: The flake-tool tradition associated mainly with Neanderthals across Europe and western Asia.

entities.name: Aterian Industry
entities.date_note: 145 +/- 9 ka is the weighted-mean thermoluminescence age at El Mnasra. The industry is defined by tool shape rather than by date, so its limits move with the definition. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A North African tradition marked by tanged points, made by early modern humans across the Sahara.

entities.name: Still Bay Industry
entities.date_note: Single-grain OSL makes this a short episode of under 5,000 years. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Diepkloof thermoluminescence chronology
alternatives.note: TL at Diepkloof puts the Still Bay some 35,000 years earlier than the single-grain OSL chronology.

entities.summary: A brief South African tradition of finely worked leaf-shaped points, an early flowering of complex technique.

entities.name: Howiesons Poort Industry
entities.date_note: Single-grain OSL makes this a tight horizon marker; ESR and TL at Klasies River give a looser 50,000-60,000 years. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. alternatives.label: Klasies River ESR/TL chronology
alternatives.note: Looser and younger than the single-grain OSL horizon.

entities.summary: A South African tradition of small backed blades, hafted as composite tools, lasting only a few thousand years.

entities.name: Later Stone Age
entities.date_note: Border Cave gives 44.2-43.0 cal BP for the earliest layer. There is no real end date: the Later Stone Age runs on into recorded history, and the value here is a convention for the tree rather than a finding. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The sub-Saharan African tradition of small composite tools that continues into the historical period.

entities.name: Châtelperronian Industry
entities.date_note: In Cantabria it shows no chronological overlap with the local Mousterian, which complicates the usual reading of it as a Neanderthal response to arriving modern humans. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A short-lived western European tradition made during the overlap between Neanderthals and modern humans.

entities.name: Aurignacian Industry
entities.date_note: Arrival dates differ sharply between regional models, from about 43 cal ka BP in southern Iberia to later elsewhere.

alternatives.label: Banks et al. 2013 phase model
alternatives.note: Proto-Aurignacian 41.5-39.9 k cal BP, Early Aurignacian 39.8-37.9 k cal BP.

entities.summary: The first widespread modern-human tradition in Europe, associated with the earliest cave art and figurines.

entities.name: Gravettian Industry
entities.date_note: Bayesian boundaries from the Adriatic basin; regional models differ.
entities.summary: The tradition of the Venus figurines and mammoth-bone dwellings, spanning Europe through the coldest part of the Ice Age.

entities.name: Solutrean Industry
entities.date_note: Bayesian analysis does not confirm the traditional ordering of the internal phases, so the sub-sequence is less secure than the overall span. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: An Iberian and French tradition known for slender, finely pressure-flaked laurel-leaf points.

entities.name: Magdalenian Industry
entities.date_note: Preceded by the Badegoulian at 23,092-20,792 cal BP. Regional phase models disagree on the internal sequence. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The late Ice Age tradition of Lascaux and Altamira, ending as the glaciers retreated.

entities.name: Göbekli Tepe
entities.date_note: Only 11 radiocarbon dates exist. The Layer III/II/I scheme has been abandoned for at least eight phases, so phase labels in older sources do not map cleanly. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: Monumental enclosures raised by people who were not yet farming, in southeastern Anatolia.

entities.name: Monte Verde II
entities.date_note: Median c. 14,530 cal BP, 95.4% range 14,200-14,900 cal BP; the span shown is the dating range, not a measured occupation length. Under active challenge: a March 2026 reanalysis proposed a Holocene age, roughly thirty specialists rebutted it in May, and the authors replied in June. The genetic models for the peopling of the Americas do not depend on the outcome either way. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Surovell et al. 2026
alternatives.note: Argues the dated material is intrusive and the occupation is mid-Holocene.

caveats.text: The site that broke Clovis First is itself under serious challenge, and the argument is live as of 2026.

entities.summary: A settlement in southern Chile whose age broke the Clovis-first model of the peopling of the Americas.

entities.name: Behavioural Firsts
entities.summary: The earliest known evidence for each human behaviour — toolmaking, fire, pigment, burial, art, seafaring. Each date is a floor, not an estimate.
entities.date_note: Starts with the contested Dikika cut marks at 3.39 Ma, which is older than the app's 3.3 Ma floor because the floor tracks the oldest ACCEPTED behaviour and Dikika is not accepted. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

entities.name: Stone Knapping
entities.date_note: THE SCOPE FLOOR, defined as a behaviour rather than as a site. Lomekwi 3 is the present evidence, not the definition: the artefacts lie above the Toroto Tuff at 3.31 +/- 0.02 Ma, within the Mammoth reverse subchron. If an older knapping site is accepted, this date moves and the app's scope does not change. Predates the oldest Homo fossil by about 500,000 years, which is why the floor is behavioural and not taxonomic. Published range extended to 3300000 BCE; recorded as a lower bound only, because a threshold can only move older.

alternatives.label: Assemblage not in primary context
alternatives.note: Argues the stratigraphic association with the dated tuff is not established. Offers no alternative date; the implied age is essentially the same. The excavators replied in 2019.

caveats.text: A minority reads the flakes as naturally fractured stone rather than deliberate knapping.

entities.summary: The first deliberate shaping of stone into tools — the behaviour this app uses to mark where human prehistory begins.

entities.name: Butchery of Animals
entities.date_note: The secure record begins 2.6-2.5 Ma at Gona and Bouri, Ethiopia. A claim for 3.39 Ma at Dikika is the older candidate and is not accepted.

alternatives.label: Dikika cut marks
alternatives.note: Marks on two bones claimed as butchery before 3.39 Ma. Critics read them as trampling: 96% of experimental trampling grooves are broad and open, against 4% of genuine cut marks.

caveats.text: The 3.39 Ma Dikika claim is widely read as trampling damage rather than butchery.

entities.summary: Cutting meat from bone with stone tools, which opened a food source that had been out of reach.

entities.name: Controlled Use of Fire
entities.date_note: Wonderwerk Cave Stratum 10 is the standard secure minimum, bracketed by cosmogenic burial ages of 1.27 +/- 0.19 and 0.98 +/- 0.19 Ma. Older claims exist and the field has not settled. Published range extended to 800000 BCE; recorded as a lower bound only, because a threshold can only move older.

alternatives.label: Wonderwerk Stratum 11
alternatives.note: A 2026 reanalysis pushes burning at the same cave back to 1.79-1.07 Ma.

alternatives.label: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov
alternatives.note: The best-evidenced repeated hearth use, fixed by the Matuyama-Brunhes reversal at 0.79 Ma. Younger than Wonderwerk but less contested.

entities.summary: Keeping and using fire on purpose, which changed diet, safety and how far north people could live.

entities.name: Cooking of Food
entities.date_note: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, from eight sequential horizons correlated to marine isotope stages 18-20. Note the long gap between the earliest fire and the earliest cooking: the two are not the same behaviour.
entities.summary: Applying controlled heat to food, evidenced by fish teeth heated to a temperature that implies cooking rather than burning.

entities.name: Use of Pigment
entities.date_note: Secure from about 300 ka in both Africa and Europe. Between 1.5 Ma and 300 ka the evidence is sparse and equivocal. Kapthurin GnJh-15 in Kenya is the earliest well-dated assemblage at 0.284 +/- 0.012 Ma.

alternatives.label: Olorgesailie worked pigment
alternatives.note: Described as the oldest clearly worked pigment.

entities.summary: Collecting and working coloured earth, the earliest hint of decoration or marking.

entities.name: Deliberate Burial
entities.date_note: Sima de los Huesos in Spain holds over 7,000 bones from at least 29 individuals, a minimum age since the dated speleothem formed directly on the deposit. Whether accumulation counts as burial is the argument. Qafzeh in Israel at 90-100 ka is the earliest undisputed grave. Published range extended to 425000 BCE; recorded as a lower bound only, because a threshold can only move older.

alternatives.label: Qafzeh, earliest undisputed grave
alternatives.note: A modern-human burial with fallow-deer antlers placed on the chest, cut into bedrock. Thermoluminescence on burnt flint.

alternatives.label: Homo naledi burial claim
alternatives.note: A 2023 claim of deliberate burial by a small-brained hominin at Rising Star, formally rebutted and not accepted.

caveats.text: Whether the Sima accumulation is burial or another process is unresolved; the Homo naledi claim is rejected by most reviewers.

entities.summary: Placing the dead somewhere on purpose rather than leaving them where they fell.

entities.name: Personal Ornaments
entities.date_note: Bizmoune Cave, Morocco: 33 pierced Tritia gibbosula shells, dated by uranium-series on a speleothem to 142,290 +29,300/-22,060 years at 2 sigma. Explicitly a minimum. Single-grain OSL on the same layer gives ages as young as 57,800 +/- 7,200, which is unresolved. Published range extended to 110000 BCE; recorded as a lower bound only, because a threshold can only move older.

alternatives.label: Bizmoune OSL chronology
alternatives.note: Optically stimulated luminescence on layer 4c returns a far younger age than the uranium-series speleothem date.

entities.summary: Shells pierced and strung to be worn, which means signalling something about yourself to other people.

entities.name: Abstract Engraving
entities.date_note: Blombos Cave, South Africa: 77 +/- 6 ka by thermoluminescence on burnt lithics for the engraved ochre, with a drawn cross-hatch in ochre crayon at about 73 ka from the same site. Published range extended to 69000 BCE; recorded as a lower bound only, because a threshold can only move older.

alternatives.label: Trinil engraved shell
alternatives.note: A zigzag engraved on a freshwater mussel shell from Java, attributed to Homo erectus. If accepted it moves this threshold back by 350,000 years.

entities.summary: Deliberate cross-hatched patterns cut into ochre — marks that mean something without depicting anything.

entities.name: Intentional Seafaring
entities.date_note: The colonisation of Sahul recorded at Madjedbebe, Australia: 65 +/- 6 ka at 95.4% by single-grain OSL with Bayesian modelling. Reaching Australia required repeated open-water crossings, so the site dates the voyage as well as the landfall. Published range extended to 57000 BCE; recorded as a lower bound only, because a threshold can only move older.

alternatives.label: Sceptical reading of the Madjedbebe chronology
alternatives.note: Critics read the same OSL data as about 53 +/- 4 ka, arguing artefacts moved down through the sand.

entities.summary: Crossing open water on purpose, out of sight of the far shore, which requires planning and a built craft.

entities.name: Figurative Art
entities.date_note: A narrative scene at Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi: a warty pig with human figures, dated by laser-ablation uranium-series on the overlying carbonate. A minimum, since the art is older than the crust that formed on it. The 2024 laser-ablation method also pushed the neighbouring Leang Bulu' Sipong 4 scene from 44 ka to about 48 ka.

alternatives.label: European Upper Palaeolithic art
alternatives.note: Chauvet's first occupation is 37,000-33,500 cal BP and the Hohle Fels ivory figurine at least 35,000 years old. Long taken as the earliest figurative art until the Sulawesi dates.

caveats.text: Often said to begin in Ice Age Europe. The oldest known figurative art is in Indonesia and predates Chauvet by some 14,000 years.

entities.summary: Pictures of recognisable things — animals and people — rather than patterns.

entities.name: Lomekwian Industry
entities.date_note: Named from Lomekwi 3. Kept separate from the Oldowan because the knapping technique differs, which is also why the Oldowan's 2.6 Ma start is a definitional boundary rather than the start of toolmaking. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The oldest known stone toolkit: large, heavy cores and flakes struck with techniques unlike the later Oldowan.

entities.name: Middle Stone Age
entities.date_note: Roughly 300-30 ka, about 270,000 years. The end is regionally staggered. Radiocarbon only reaches the terminal MSA; everything older rests on OSL, TL, ESR and uranium-series, whose ages are quoted as 'BP' but are not radiocarbon and need no calibration. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Jacobs & Roberts maximum-age chronology
alternatives.note: Single-grain OSL compresses the diagnostic sub-industries into brief horizons; TL and ESR readings stretch them.

entities.summary: The long African toolmaking tradition during which our own species appeared, and with it pigment, beads and engraving.

entities.name: African Prehistory
entities.date_note: Africa holds the whole span. The hominin species themselves sit under Human Prehistory rather than here, because a species is not a region's property; this branch holds African sites and cultures. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The continent where the human story begins, and where it stays for most of its length.

entities.name: Olduvai Gorge
entities.date_note: Bed I begins immediately above the Naabi Ignimbrite at 2.038 +/- 0.005 Ma. The sequence runs up through Beds II to IV. Among the best-constrained chronologies in African prehistory, with errors of a few thousand years. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A Tanzanian ravine cutting through two million years of deposits, the site that made early human archaeology a dated science.

entities.name: Omo Kibish
entities.date_note: Omo I is older than 233 +/- 22 ka, dated by single-crystal Ar/Ar on sanidine from the overlying KHS Tuff. A minimum: no robust maximum age exists. The date changed in 2022 because the anchoring tephra was reidentified, not because the method improved.
entities.summary: The Ethiopian site of Omo I, for decades the oldest known fossil of our own species.

entities.name: Blombos Cave
entities.date_note: Occupation from 98.9 +/- 4.5 ka to a sterile hiatus sand at 67.8 +/- 4.2 ka, on single-grain OSL. TL on burnt lithics agrees within error. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A South African cave holding engraved ochre, shell beads and the oldest known drawing.

entities.name: Klasies River Mouth
entities.date_note: Base dated by uranium-disequilibrium to about 110 ka, the LBS member corresponding to the Last Interglacial. The top of the MSA sequence is beyond the radiocarbon limit, so 50 ka is a floor rather than an end. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: The chronology is broadly accepted; what is argued is whether the fragmentary human remains are fully modern.

entities.summary: A South African cave sequence with some of the earliest anatomically modern human remains outside East Africa.

entities.name: Border Cave
entities.date_note: The 200 ka start rests on ESR. The Early Later Stone Age horizon is 44.2-43.0 ka cal BP by AMS radiocarbon. Occupation continues into the Holocene, so the end here is a convention. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Conventional Later Stone Age onset
alternatives.note: Villa and Beaumont put the LSA onset here at 44-42 ka cal BP, roughly 20,000 years earlier than the conventional figure elsewhere.

entities.summary: A South African site whose sequence runs from the Middle Stone Age into the present, including the earliest Later Stone Age toolkit.

entities.name: Green Sahara
entities.date_note: Onset about 14.5 ka with the Bolling-Allerod warming, at the end of Heinrich Event 1. Termination is time-transgressive rather than a single event: the northern and eastern Sahara dried after 8-7 ka while other areas stayed wet, and parts of the Sahel, Arabia and East Africa stayed wet until about the 4.2 ka event. Independent syntheses put the window at 14,800-5,500 and 14,500-5,000 years ago; the difference is framing rather than disagreement. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Abrupt termination
alternatives.note: deMenocal's marine-core reading has the end as an abrupt step; reanalyses argue for a gradual, regionally staggered dry-down.

entities.summary: The window when the Sahara held lakes, rivers and grassland, and people lived across what is now the largest hot desert on Earth.

entities.name: Nabta Playa
entities.date_note: Early Neolithic from 10,800 cal BP; abandoned to hyperaridity at about 6,200 cal BP as the Green Sahara ended. MIND THE CALIBRATION: the excavation literature reports the later ceremonial phases as bare radiocarbon BP, not calibrated, and on that scale gives abandonment at about 5,400 BP. The two numbers are the same event in two conventions, not two readings of the evidence. The phase entries below carry the uncalibrated figures as published rather than silently converting them. alternatives.note: Malville's Late-to-Terminal Neolithic span, published as raw BP.

caveats.text: The cultural chronology is reasonably settled. The claim that the megaliths are astronomically aligned is not.
Its early Holocene cattle bones are widely cited as independent African domestication; they are argued to be hunted wild aurochs.

entities.summary: A seasonal lake basin in the Egyptian Sahara with cattle burials and a megalithic circle, occupied while the desert was green.

entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON, as published. Ends in a short but deep drought beginning about 7,600 BP and lasting roughly a century. entities.name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A
entities.date_note: 9800/9700 to 8800/8700 cal BC in the PPND scheme, from about 800 compiled radiocarbon dates. entities.name: Domestic Dog
entities.date_note: Oldest confirmed genetic evidence is 15,800-14,200 years ago, from sites in Britain and Turkiye. Successive ancient-genome studies have pushed this progressively earlier, and a Palaeolithic origin is now firm even though the exact date and place are not.

entities.date_note: 13,700-11,700 cal BP. The Natufian is pre-agricultural, so this predates domesticated cereals by millennia.

entities.name: Cereal Domestication
entities.date_note: 10,600-9,900 cal BP for the earliest definite domesticated wheat. Barley follows at Tell Aswad, 10,200-9,550 cal BP. A 2025 genetic study puts the domestication-associated barley haplotype as much as 27,000 years old, which no archaeobotanical evidence supports; that gap is unresolved.
entities.summary: Einkorn and emmer wheat at Cayonu and Cafer Hoyuk: the beginning of the crop package that spread across three continents.

entities.name: Woven Cloth
entities.summary: Preserved woven textile from Catalhoyuk — spinning and weaving, as distinct from the far older twisting of fibre into cord.

entities.name: Irrigation
entities.date_note: Samarra culture, c. 6200-5700 BC.
entities.summary: Canals and ditches at Choga Mami in Mesopotamia, the first farming that reshaped the land to suit itself.

entities.name: The Wheel
entities.date_note: Uruk pictographs c. 3500-3350 BCE and the Bronocice pot at 3635-3370 cal BCE are effectively contemporaneous. entities.summary: Wheeled wagons appear in Mesopotamia and central Europe at nearly the same moment, and which came first is unresolved.

entities.name: Writing
entities.date_note: Mesopotamian proto-cuneiform c. 3400-3200 BCE; the Abydos tomb U-j tags c. 3320 BCE. The ranges overlap and the two systems developed independently, so neither is assigned priority here.

alternatives.label: Egyptian priority (Abydos tomb U-j)
alternatives.note: Bone and ivory tags bearing early hieroglyphic signs, Naqada III.

caveats.text: Not a single invention that spread: Mesopotamian and Egyptian writing arose independently within overlapping date ranges.

entities.summary: Proto-cuneiform at Uruk and hieroglyphic tags at Abydos — two independent inventions whose dates overlap.

entities.name: Horse Domestication
entities.date_note: The DOM2 lineage emerges c. 2200 BCE and spreads rapidly after 2000 BC. Botai horses, c. 3500 BC, remain the earliest known husbandry but are a genetic dead end — Przewalski's ancestry, not ours. The two answer different questions and conflating them is the usual error.

caveats.text: Botai is still widely cited as the origin of domestic horses; genomics showed in 2021 that it is not.

entities.summary: The ancestry of every modern domestic horse traces to the lower Volga-Don steppe, not to the older Botai husbandry once assumed to be its origin.

entities.name: Domestic Chicken
entities.date_note: First unambiguous domestic chicken bones at Ban Non Wat, Thailand, 1650-1250 BCE. Chickens reach South Asia and Mesopotamia only in the late 2nd millennium BCE, and Mediterranean Europe around 800 BCE.

entities.summary: The world's most numerous bird was domesticated in mainland Southeast Asia, far later and further east than long assumed.
