alternatives.label: The basin is a reservoir, not a dock
alternatives.note: Leshnik argued in 1968 that it held drinking or irrigation water and that ship draught requirements were never met. Possehl noted the absence of a hinterland and of shipbuilding remains.

entities.summary: A small Gujarat settlement with a large baked-brick basin that has been argued over for sixty years: dockyard, or reservoir?

entities.name: Rakhigarhi
entities.date_note: AMS dates on charcoal at 20.6 m and 9.1 m depth give 2616+/-73 and 2273+/-38 cal BCE. The cemetery is dated 2500-2000 BCE. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The largest Harappan site by area, and the source of the only ancient genome yet recovered from within the civilisation.

entities.name: The Rakhigarhi Genome
entities.date_note: Dated by association, not directly. Five attempts to radiocarbon-date the individual's own remains failed on carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, so the only anchor is seven charcoal dates from the habitation area, 2800-2300 BCE. There is no calibrated date for the woman herself. The authors caution that one genome cannot characterise a cosmopolitan civilisation, and that a fitting model need not be the true source population.

caveats.text: Widely reported as disproving Indo-Aryan migration. It does not. It shows no steppe ancestry in one mature-period individual, which the companion paper agrees with.

entities.summary: A single woman's DNA, recovered after 61 attempts, showed the Harappans carried no steppe ancestry and no Anatolian farmer ancestry.

entities.name: Arrival of Steppe Ancestry in South Asia
entities.date_note: Not an excavated date but a genetic admixture estimate: in Swat individuals the relevant mixture dates to a 95% interval of roughly 1900-1500 BCE, 26 generations before they lived. Steppe ancestry is undetectable in South Asia before 2000 BCE. This dates a population mixture, not a language or an invasion; the authors state the path by which the ancestry arrived is uncertain, and some archaeologists see too few material-culture links between the Central Steppe and South Asia to accept a connection at all. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The window in which steppe pastoralist ancestry entered South Asia, after the Harappan cities had already emptied.

entities.name: Harappan Deurbanisation
entities.date_note: An Arabian Sea isotope record shows rainfall and Indus discharge dropping abruptly at 4.2 ka, with the sharpest change at 4.1 ka. A 2023 study resolves this into a 230-year run of drought pulses centred at 4.19, 4.11 and 4.02 ka.

alternatives.label: Gradual decline from about 2500 BCE
alternatives.note: Giosan and colleagues argue the monsoon weakened progressively rather than failing at one moment, and that a separate winter-monsoon decline around 1300-1000 BCE affected the late phase as well.

entities.summary: The cities are abandoned over roughly three centuries as the monsoon weakens and inundation agriculture stops paying.

entities.name: The Ghaggar-Hakra Question
entities.date_note: Isotope work on Rann of Kachchh cores puts the last Himalayan glacier-fed river reaching the sea at roughly 10,000 years ago, which is several millennia before the Harappan period. Proposed desiccation dates for the later monsoon-fed channel range from the mid-4th millennium BCE to 1400 BCE. The timing is unresolved and consequential: a pre-Harappan drying cannot have caused a collapse that had not happened yet. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: The river did not vanish overnight. The described process is a centuries-long shrinkage from a perennial glacier-fed river to an intermittent monsoon-fed one.

entities.summary: Whether a great river dried and took the cities with it. The geology says the big glacier-fed river was already gone long before the cities existed.

name_forms.name: Sarasvati question
name_forms.note: Names the debate after the Vedic river, which is the claim the debate is about.

name_forms.name: Ghaggar-Hakra
name_forms.note: The modern hydronym, used because it does not presuppose the identification.

entities.name: The Indus Script
entities.date_note: Earliest writing is attested in the Kot Dijian phase at Harappa, 2800-2600 BCE, with potter's marks earlier still. The developed script runs through the mature period to about 1900 BCE. The writing question is still open after twenty years: the most recent work finds the corpus sits between the linguistic and non-linguistic baselines, matching neither. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Not a writing system
alternatives.note: Farmer, Sproat and Witzel argued in 2004 that inscriptions are too short and that no scribal class or writing equipment has been found. Rao replied that entropy resembles language.

entities.summary: Undeciphered, and still argued over at a more basic level: whether the signs encode language at all.

entities.name: Southern Neolithic
entities.date_note: Three phases in the Allchin framework: 2500-2000, 2000-1600 and 1600-1000 BC. A second published scheme gives 2300-1800 and 1800-1200 cal BC for the later two. Both are in use; they are not averaged here.

caveats.text: Not among the world's early Neolithic transitions, and not the earliest in South Asia. It begins in the 3rd millennium BC, well after the northwest.

entities.summary: A separate Neolithic in the South Deccan, built on cattle, native millets and enormous mounds of burnt dung.

entities.name: The Ashmounds
entities.date_note: AMS dates and stratigraphy at the Sanganakallu complex put ash formation between 1950 and 1750 BC, over perhaps less than 200 years. Village activity then continued on top of the mounds for another 500-700 years. That the deposits are burnt dung is chemically settled; why the dung was burned is not, with proposals from disease control in pens to ritual. Only some mounds are dated: Kudatini and Budihal are placed by settlement typology rather than radiocarbon, so no dates are stated for them. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: Mounds of burnt cattle dung, some many metres high, built up by repeated firing of cattle pens over less than two centuries.

entities.name: South Indian Millet Domestication
entities.date_note: The staples are Brachiaria ramosa and Setaria, both native South Indian species, present with mung bean and horsegram from the earliest levels. African pearl millet and finger millet arrive later, as introductions.

caveats.text: An early claim that sorghum straw appears in ashmound slag near Kudatini is rejected by later systematic archaeobotany, which found no sorghum at all.

entities.summary: Browntop and foxtail millet with mung bean and horsegram, argued to be domesticated in peninsular India rather than introduced.

entities.name: Burzahom
entities.date_note: Eight charcoal dates run at TIFR in 1965-66, MASCA-calibrated, give an aceramic phase about 3000-2850 BCE, early ceramic 2850-2550, late ceramic 2550-1700, and a megalithic phase 1500-1000 BCE. The raw TF-series figures are uncalibrated and use a 5730-year half-life; mixing them with the MASCA-calibrated boundaries shifts the site by centuries.
entities.summary: A Kashmir valley site of pit dwellings cut into loess, with a Neolithic sequence running into a megalithic phase.

entities.name: Late Pleistocene China
entities.date_note: A container era. The span runs from the earliest directly dated modern human in the region to the start of the Neolithic sequence; each entry below carries its own dating. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: China before farming: the earliest modern human remains in the region, and foragers making pottery thousands of years before any crop.

entities.name: Tianyuan Cave
entities.date_note: 34,430+/-510 BP uncalibrated on the femur, calibrating to 38,120-40,940 cal BP. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A femur near Beijing from one of the earliest directly dated modern humans in East Asia.

entities.name: Xianrendong Cave
entities.date_note: Ten AMS dates put the lowest sherd-bearing levels at 20,000-19,000 cal BP, which would be 2,000-3,000 years older than any other pottery known. Two independent re-analyses dispute this. The range authored here is Kuzmin's more conservative re-derivation; the Science figure is carried below. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Pottery at 20,000-19,000 cal BP
alternatives.note: The original Science claim, from the excavating team. Peer-reviewed, and disputed by two later peer-reviewed re-analyses.

caveats.text: Reported almost everywhere as settled. It is not: specialists argue the dates have obscure context, conflict with the TL dates on the ceramics, and disagree with the palaeoclimate.

entities.summary: A Jiangxi cave holding what may be the oldest pottery in the world, made by foragers during the Last Glacial Maximum — if the dates hold.

entities.name: Yuchanyan Cave
entities.date_note: The 2009 study dates the pottery to 18,300-15,430 cal BP, with the most secure earliest estimate at 18,300-17,500 cal BP. It was built around dating the association itself rather than the layer, which is why it is preferred here over the older lab results. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Older lab results, c. 17,200-14,700 cal BP
alternatives.note: Zhao and Wu's 2000 figures, calibrated. Younger than the dedicated 2009 study and based on less controlled associations.

entities.summary: A Hunan cave with early pottery and wild rice, dated by a study designed specifically to get the chronology right.

entities.name: Cishan Culture
entities.date_note: The contested part is not the culture but its earliest millet. Three AMS dates were reported at 10,400-10,100 cal BP, which would put broomcorn millet cultivation near 10,000 BP. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Millet cultivation from c. 10,400 cal BP
alternatives.note: Zhao's critique argues the samples' archaeological context does not support the claim. The earliest DIRECT date on millet grains anywhere in the region is 5670-5610 BCE, at Xinglongwa.

caveats.text: The very early millet dates are widely repeated as the origin of north Chinese agriculture. They are described in the literature as highly controversial on sample-context grounds.

entities.summary: A north China millet culture whose storage pits produced the claim that cereal farming here began at the Pleistocene boundary.

entities.name: Xinglongwa Culture
entities.date_note: Flourishes after 8.2 ka cal BP in the regional sequence. Its significance for dating is the direct AMS date on millet grains, 5670-5610 BCE — the conservative anchor against which the disputed Cishan claims are measured. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A northeast China culture of planned villages, jade working, and the earliest millet grains anywhere to be dated directly rather than by context.

entities.name: Dawenkou Culture
entities.date_note: Conventionally 4300-2600 BCE in three phases. A Bayesian re-modelling puts the onset at 4500-3900 BCE and the end considerably later, at 2100-1800 BCE; the two schemes differ by centuries at both ends.
entities.summary: An eastern China culture of elaborate burials and incised pottery marks sometimes discussed, carefully, in relation to later Chinese writing.

entities.name: Hemudu Culture
entities.date_note: Radiocarbon places first occupation about 5000-4900 BCE and the main village ending about 4600 BCE. An independent paleomagnetic chronology gives a start near 7000 cal BP, which agrees once units are reconciled but rests on an entirely different method. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: Paleomagnetic chronology, from c. 7000 cal BP
alternatives.note: Zheng et al. 2021, derived from sediment magnetism rather than radiocarbon.

entities.summary: A waterlogged lower Yangtze site that preserved wooden mortise-and-tenon architecture and some of the earliest cultivated rice.

entities.name: Daxi Culture
entities.date_note: Full rice agriculture is established in the middle Yangtze in this period, about 6400-5300 BP. Fortification at Chengtoushan appears as early as 6400-6100 cal BP. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A middle Yangtze culture with some of the earliest walled settlements in China, at Chengtoushan.

entities.name: Shijiahe Culture
entities.date_note: AMS phases: early 4850-4400 cal BP, middle 4400-4200, late 4200-4000. Rice grains from Shijiahe contexts date to 2580-2340 and 2480-2280 cal BC. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A middle Yangtze late Neolithic culture of walled settlements and rice, contemporary with Longshan further north.

entities.name: Qijia Culture
entities.date_note: Credible academic sources give ranges from about 2400/2250 BCE to as late as 1400 BCE for different sub-sites and phases. The Mogou site specifically dates to 1750-1400 BC. This is real heterogeneity within the culture rather than a dating error, and no single range represents the whole. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A northwest culture straddling the Neolithic and Bronze Age, central to arguments about how metallurgy reached China.

entities.name: The Liangzhu Hydraulic System
entities.date_note: AMS on grass from the sandbags used in construction, plus associated charcoal. High dams begin about 5200-4800 cal BP and low dams and levees about 5000-4800 cal BP — both before most of the walled city itself, which dates to 4900-4600 cal BP. The waterworks came first. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: Eleven dams and levees around the Liangzhu city, the earliest large-scale water management known anywhere.

entities.name: Erlitou
entities.date_note: Wiggle-matched radiocarbon compresses the occupation to roughly 1750-1520 BCE, about two centuries. The date has moved repeatedly: broadly 2100-1300 BC on 20th-century radiocarbon, 1880-1520 BC from the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project, about 1900-1500 BC in the general literature, and later still after Wu Xiaohong's 2007 work on lower-layer samples. There is also a middle position: Liu Li and Chen Xingcan read phase II as state-level organisation but prefer the neutral label 'the Erlitou State', on the grounds that Chinese scholarship has spent too much effort on dynastic labelling and too little on craft production and settlement patterns. These are the 2007 accelerator-mass-spectrometry figures. Earlier radiocarbon work gave c.1900-1500 BCE and Britannica still prints 1900-1350. The redating matters for the Xia question in the opposite direction to the one usually assumed: it pushes Erlitou later, so the site was still developing when the Xia is conventionally said to have ended, which makes identifying the two harder.

alternatives.label: Erlitou is the Xia dynasty
alternatives.note: Held by most Chinese scholars and some overseas. The Chronology Project assigned all four Erlitou phases to Xia and dated Xia's start to c. 2070 BCE.

caveats.text: Most overseas scholars hold that Erlitou cannot be identified as Xia without contemporaneous writing. Shang oracle bones show no sign of a Xia concept; the name first appears in Zhou texts.
Chinese archaeologists generally read Erlitou as the Xia's material remains. No contemporary writing confirms it — the earliest Chinese script is late Shang.

entities.summary: A large early Bronze Age centre in Henan with palace foundations and bronze workshops, and the site the entire Xia argument is actually about.

entities.name: Chulmun Period
entities.date_note: Schemes disagree on both ends. A four-phase calendar scheme runs 7500-1300 BC; a three-phase cal BP scheme runs 7500-3400 cal BP; another source puts the Korean Neolithic's start near 10,000 BP. The range here is a conservative middle of the published schemes, not an average of them. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: Korea's Neolithic: comb-patterned pottery, coastal foraging, and the slow arrival of millet from northeast China.

name_forms.name: Jeulmun pottery period
name_forms.note: Revised Romanization spelling. Korean romanisation changed system in 2000, so the same word appears two ways across the literature.

entities.name: Arrival of Millet in Korea
entities.date_note: The earliest secure direct AMS date on a millet grain is 3640-3370 cal BC. Corroborating grains date to 3520, 3360 and 2970 cal BC. A 2025 Bayesian estimate gives a much wider 90% interval of 5772-3490 cal BCE, which is an uncertainty range and not a claim of an earlier arrival. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: Foxtail and broomcorn millet reach the peninsula from northeast China, Korea's first cultivated cereals and some two millennia before rice.

entities.name: Mumun Period
entities.date_note: Commonly given as 1500-300 BC, with early Mumun 1500-800 BC and middle Mumun 800-400 BC. Three directly AMS-dated middle Mumun individuals fall at 770-410 cal BC. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: Korea's Bronze Age transition: undecorated pottery, megalithic burial, and the arrival of paddy rice from the Liaodong route.

entities.name: Arrival of Rice in Korea
entities.date_note: Associated with the start of Mumun around 1500 BCE, or about 1300 BCE on an archaeolinguistic reading. The earliest directly dated rice grains, from Oun-1 at Jinju, are calibrated two different ways from the SAME samples: 2860-1320 cal BC by one treatment and 1950-1000 cal BC by another. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: Claims of Pleistocene rice in Korea, such as Sorori at 17,000-13,000 BP, describe disputed 'quasi-rice' and are not evidence of cultivation.

entities.summary: Paddy rice reaches Korea by a Shandong-Liaodong route, the agricultural change that would shortly cross to Japan and begin the Yayoi.

entities.name: Sannai Maruyama
entities.date_note: Occupied about 5900-4300 cal BP, corroborated across four independently published sources. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: Its scale is often read as implying agriculture. The economy was foraging-based, which is precisely why the site matters for arguments about sedentism without farming.

entities.summary: A large, long-lived Jomon settlement with monumental timber posts and long-distance exchange, built by people who were not farmers.

entities.name: The Late Jomon Population Decline
entities.date_note: Summed radiocarbon probability over 1,598 Late Jomon dates (4420-3220 cal BP) and 1,462 Final Jomon dates (3220-2300 cal BP) shows decline and plateau, with regional troughs at 3900-3800 cal BP in Kanto and 3800-3500 cal BP in Aomori and Hokkaido. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: Koyama's often-quoted population figures are site-density extrapolations, not counts derived from dated remains. The radiocarbon curve is the citable evidence for the timing.

entities.summary: A sustained demographic contraction across the Japanese archipelago, centuries before wet rice arrived.

entities.name: The Yayoi Redating Controversy
entities.date_note: The traditional start was the 5th-4th century BCE. In May 2003 the National Museum of Japanese History dated charred residue on pottery and argued for the 10th century BCE. Positions since: no earlier than the 9th century (Miyamoto); no earlier than the 8th (Takesue, Shoda); outright rejection and retention of the 5th (Takakura, Hashiguchi). By 2010 most Japanese archaeologists had accepted the direction of the shift without agreeing on its size. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

alternatives.label: 10th century BCE (NMJH, 2003)
alternatives.note: The original proposal, from AMS dates on charred residue. Supported in direction by paddy-field dating in northern Kyushu.

alternatives.label: 9th-8th century BCE
alternatives.note: Miyamoto allows no earlier than the 9th century; Takesue and Shoda no earlier than the 8th, on cross-dating rather than AMS.

alternatives.label: Traditional 5th century BCE
alternatives.note: The pre-2003 consensus, retained by Takakura and Hashiguchi, who rejected the redating outright.

caveats.text: Not a dispute about whether AMS dating works. The criticisms are that the redating altered the type-definitions it depended on, and that the pottery itself was misidentified.

entities.summary: In 2003 a national museum used AMS dating to move the start of the Yayoi back five centuries, and the field has still not settled where it lands.

entities.name: Uruk Period
entities.date_note: Four frameworks are in circulation and disagree: CDLI gives 4000-3000 BC on stratigraphy; ARCANE gives Early and Middle Uruk 4200-3800 and Late Uruk 3800-3000 on calibrated radiocarbon; ISAC's LC scheme gives Middle Uruk 3700-3400 and Late Uruk 3400-3100; Unicode's script phases run 3500-3000. They are not averaged here.

caveats.text: Older literature dates Uruk IVa as late as 2815 BC. ARCANE notes those figures rest on uncalibrated or incorrect readings; the calibrated cluster is around 3450 BC.

entities.summary: The centuries in which southern Mesopotamia produced the first cities, the first bureaucracy, and the first writing.

name_forms.name: Unug
name_forms.note: The city's Sumerian name, written 𒀕𒆠. Uruk is the Akkadian form.

name_forms.name: Erech
name_forms.note: The biblical form, and how the name first reached English.

name_forms.name: Warka
name_forms.note: The modern Arabic name of the site, possibly the root of 'Iraq'.

entities.name: Uruk
entities.date_note: Sizes are from archaeological survey, not radiocarbon. Uruk grows from under 10 ha before the period to about 70 ha at its start and about 100 ha at its end, reaching roughly 400 ha in the Early Dynastic period.

caveats.text: Figures of 250 to 600 hectares and populations of 40,000 circulate widely. Only the CDLI survey figures trace to an institution, and no population estimate traces to anything.

entities.summary: The first city: about 100 hectares by the end of the period, holding more than half the settled area of southern Mesopotamia around it.

entities.name: The Uruk Expansion
entities.date_note: Dated by the appearance and disappearance of southern Mesopotamian material at northern sites, not independently. Four readings are current: colonisation, peaceful trade, displaced migration, and rejection of the whole model in favour of independent northern development.

alternatives.label: Not an expansion: independent northern development
alternatives.note: Holds that northern complexity arose on its own and the shared material reflects contact rather than any southern system.

entities.summary: Uruk material culture appears across Syria and into Anatolia, and scholars have argued for forty years about what that means.

entities.name: Proto-Cuneiform
entities.date_note: Dated to Uruk IV and III script phases, c. 3350-3000 BC. The basis is stratigraphic inference plus palaeography, not excavation context: nearly 5,000 archaic tablets came out of rubbish and fill deposits beneath Level III construction, so they must predate it, and no tablets occur below Level IV. Sign-form evolution does the rest of the work. Writing outlasts the Uruk period proper, continuing into Jemdet Nasr.

alternatives.label: Descended from clay accounting tokens
alternatives.note: Schmandt-Besserat's model: tokens, then sealed clay envelopes, then numerical tablets, then writing. Popular, and under sustained statistical attack.

caveats.text: The earliest tablets were not found in use-contexts. They came from rubbish and fill, so their date is inferred from the layers above them and from sign shapes.
Tokens were not replaced by writing. They continue in use alongside tablets, seals and tags into the 1st millennium BC.

entities.summary: The earliest known writing: numerals and word-signs pressed into clay at Uruk, used almost entirely for accounting.

entities.name: Jemdet Nasr Period
entities.summary: The short period between Uruk and the Early Dynastic, in which writing spreads beyond Uruk and becomes recognisably cuneiform.

entities.name: Proto-Elamite
entities.date_note: Roughly 3300-2900 BCE. Precision beyond that is not currently achievable: the relevant radiocarbon dates fall on a plateau in the calibration curve, which is a physical limit rather than a shortage of samples. The tablet sub-phases are relative only. It begins slightly before the Elam era node, which starts at the conventional 3200 BCE.
entities.summary: Southwestern Iran's own writing system, invented within a century or two of Mesopotamia's and still undeciphered.

entities.name: Linear Elamite
entities.date_note: Dated by the royal names appearing in the texts. The core corpus is often given as 2100-1900 BC; the 2022 decipherment paper uses 2300-1880 BCE.

alternatives.label: Not descended from Proto-Elamite
alternatives.note: Dahl argues later scribes deliberately built an archaising script from recovered Proto-Elamite tablets, as differentiation from Mesopotamia, rather than inheriting one.

caveats.text: Widely reported as deciphered. Acceptance is qualified rather than universal, and no fetched source reports a consensus statement.

entities.summary: A later Iranian script, claimed in 2022 to have been deciphered as the oldest purely phonographic writing known.

entities.name: Old Elamite Period
entities.date_note: Two incompatible schemes are in current use. The dates here follow Gasche et al.'s short chronology as used by Encyclopaedia Iranica, 2400-1450 BCE. The traditional scheme labels the same span 'Old Elamite' at 2700-1500 BCE. Reconstruction rests on a Babylonian king-list tablet found at Susa listing twelve Awan then twelve Simashkean kings.
entities.summary: Elam's first documented dynasties — Awan, Simaški, Sukkalmah — locked in alternating war and marriage with Akkad, Ur and Babylon.

entities.name: Middle Elamite Period
entities.date_note: Iranica's short chronology gives 1450-1050 BCE, UNESCO gives 1400-1100, and other reference works give 1500-1100. Three institutional sources, three ranges, not reconciled and not averaged.
entities.summary: Elam at its most powerful, building Chogha Zanbil and carrying Babylonian monuments home as loot — including the Code of Hammurabi.

entities.name: Chogha Zanbil
entities.date_note: Founded about 1250 BCE by Untash-Napirisha and destroyed by Ashurbanipal about 640 BCE. The ziggurat was 105.2 m per side and about 53 m tall; 24.75 m survives.

alternatives.label: Untash-Napirisha reigned c. 1340-1300 BCE
alternatives.note: Follows from Iranica's cross-date to Burnaburiaš II. UNESCO instead gives 1275-1240. Which is right depends on which Kassite king the Berlin Letter means.

entities.summary: A royal city built around the best-preserved ziggurat in Iran, abandoned unfinished with thousands of unused bricks still on site.

name_forms.name: Dur-Untash
name_forms.note: 'Fortress of Untash', its Elamite name, stamped on its own bricks.

name_forms.name: Chogha Zanbil
name_forms.note: The modern Persian name of the mound, roughly 'basket hill'.

name_forms.name: Tchogha Zanbil
name_forms.note: The French transliteration, used by UNESCO.

entities.name: Neo-Elamite Period
entities.date_note: Potts gives 1000-539 BC and Iranica 1050-539. The internal boundaries differ more: the Neo-Elamite I/II line is placed at 744, 770 or 743 BC depending on the scholar. Susa fell to Ashurbanipal in 646 BC and the period ends with Cyrus in 539.

caveats.text: Elamite history here is written almost entirely from Assyrian royal inscriptions and Babylonian chronicles. Iranica calls the reconstruction a prisoner of those sources.

entities.summary: Elam's last independent centuries, spent largely in coalition against Assyria, and known mostly through Assyrian accounts of defeating it.

entities.name: Susa
entities.date_note: Remains span 4200 BCE to the Islamic period; Acropolis buildings date to at least 4000 BCE. Iranica frames the specifically Elamite phase as 2400-539 BCE, which is the range that matches this entity's parent.
entities.summary: Occupied for six thousand years, capital of Elam, and the place the Code of Hammurabi was found — because the Elamites took it there.

name_forms.name: Susa
name_forms.note: The Greek form, which is how Europe received the name.

name_forms.name: Shush
name_forms.note: The modern Iranian town on the site.

entities.name: The Hittites
entities.date_note: About 1650-1190 BCE. The basis is textual — royal annals and the Telipinu Proclamation, cross-referenced to Mesopotamian synchronisms — not radiocarbon, so the whole sequence shifts with whichever Mesopotamian chronology is adopted.
entities.summary: An Anatolian empire that fought Egypt to a draw at Kadesh and left the oldest surviving international peace treaty.

entities.name: Hittite Old Kingdom
entities.date_note: The Middle Kingdom that follows is deliberately not authored: the literature describes it as an ill-defined dark age between Telipinu and Suppiluliuma I and declines to bound it.
entities.summary: Hattusa becomes the capital and Hittite armies reach Babylon.

entities.name: Mursili I Sacks Babylon
entities.date_note: 1595 BCE on the Middle Chronology, which is the usual default. The competing schemes put it at 1736, 1651, 1587, 1531 or 1499 BCE — a spread of 237 years. Nothing about this event is independently dated; it is a king-list synchronism.

alternatives.label: Long Chronology, 1651 BCE
alternatives.note: Favoured by some astronomical reconstructions of the Venus Tablet.

alternatives.label: Short Chronology, 1531 BCE
alternatives.note: One of the lower readings of the same Venus observations.

caveats.text: 1595 BCE is quoted almost everywhere as simply the date. It is one scheme's answer to a periodic astronomical record that fits several real years equally well.

entities.summary: A Hittite raid ends Hammurabi's dynasty, and the date it happened is the hinge the whole Bronze Age chronology turns on.

entities.name: Hattusa

caveats.text: Hattusa is usually said to have been burned at the empire's end. German Archaeological Institute evidence does not support violent destruction; buildings were deliberately emptied first.

entities.summary: The Hittite capital, source of the royal archives, and — contrary to the story everyone tells — probably not sacked.

entities.name: Battle of Kadesh
entities.date_note: Year 5 of Ramesses II, which is 1274 BCE on the Egyptian Low Chronology and about twenty years earlier on the High. The treaty follows in his Year 21, usually 1259 BCE.
entities.summary: Hittites and Egyptians fight the best-documented battle of the Bronze Age to a stalemate, then sign a treaty a copy of which hangs at the UN.

entities.name: Collapse of the Hittite Empire
entities.date_note: The political collapse is dated textually. The drought is not: tree-ring widths and stable carbon isotopes in Gordion juniper place a severe multi-year dry event at 1198-1196 BCE, which is a far more precise date than anything in the political record it is being matched to.
entities.summary: The empire dissolves in the first quarter of the 12th century, during a drought that tree rings date to three specific years.

entities.name: Neo-Hittite States
entities.date_note: The end is unusually well dated because Assyria recorded each annexation: Til Barsip 856, Arpad 740, Patin 738, Damascus 732, Hamath 720, Carchemish 717, Malatya 712, Gurgum 711, and Kummuh last in 708 BCE.
entities.summary: Luwian- and Aramaic-speaking successor kingdoms that kept Hittite hieroglyphs alive for four centuries after the empire died.

entities.name: Mitanni
entities.date_note: Published ranges run from 1650-1275 to 1500-1360 BCE. Its foundation is anchored relative to the sack of Babylon — one or two generations before it — so the uncertainty is inherited wholesale from the Mesopotamian chronology problem rather than being about Mitanni at all.
entities.summary: A Hurrian kingdom of northern Syria, rival and then in-law to both Egypt and Hatti, which left the world's oldest horse-training manual.

entities.name: Urartu
entities.date_note: Dated from Urartian royal inscriptions synchronised to Assyrian annals. Sarduri I's reign is given as 844-828, 840-830, 835-825 or 834-828 BCE across reputable sources. The collapse date could not be confirmed against a fetched source and the end year here should be treated as approximate.
entities.summary: An Iron Age kingdom around Lake Van, Assyria's most persistent northern rival, built on fortresses and irrigation.

entities.name: Phrygia
entities.date_note: Midas appears as Mita of Mushki in Sargon II's annals in 717 and 709 BCE, so he is a historically attested king rather than only a legend. Gordion's absolute chronology rests on a tree-ring sequence whose end date has been revised repeatedly: 751 BCE on a decadal wiggle-match in 2010, then 745 +/- 4 BCE on annual radiocarbon in 2020. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: The Midas Mound Tumulus is not Midas's tomb. Its timber dates to about 740 BCE and Assyrian records show Midas still alive in 709.

entities.summary: An Anatolian kingdom centred on Gordion whose king Midas turns out to be documented in Assyrian records.

entities.name: Lydia
entities.summary: A western Anatolian kingdom rich enough on electrum to invent coined money, ending when Cyrus took Sardis.

entities.name: The Invention of Coinage
entities.date_note: About 650 BCE. The basis is numismatic rather than scientific: hoard finds, chiefly the foundation deposit under the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, combined with die and style sequencing. Re-filed from `event` to `threshold`: the earlier kind misdescribed what this is. Published range extended to 600 BCE; recorded as a lower bound only, because a threshold can only move older. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: Croesus did not invent coinage. Electrum coin began under Alyattes or earlier; Croesus introduced a bimetallic pure gold and silver standard a century later.

entities.summary: Struck electrum pieces of guaranteed weight appear in Lydia, and money stops having to be weighed out.

entities.name: Troy
entities.date_note: Levels I to IX span roughly 3000 BCE to 500 CE. The basis is ceramic cross-dating to Mycenaean imports, supported by over 160 radiocarbon measurements, but the site's own published table warns that precise absolute dates are not always possible. Troy VIIa's destruction is bracketed to 1260-1240 BCE on imported pottery.

alternatives.label: Homeric Troy is level VI, not VIIa
alternatives.note: VI has the monumental fortifications but appears to end in an earthquake. VIIa is a poorer rebuild showing crowding and a violent destruction, which is why Blegen preferred it.

caveats.text: Whether any Trojan War happened at all, as against a poetic composite of several conflicts, is a separate and equally unresolved question.

entities.summary: Nine cities stacked on one mound at Hisarlik, one of which may or may not be Homer's.

name_forms.name: Ilion
name_forms.note: The name behind the Iliad; Wilusa in Hittite records.

name_forms.name: Hisarlik
name_forms.note: The modern Turkish name of the mound. Excavation reports use it precisely because it does not assume the identification.

entities.name: Dilmun
entities.date_note: Dated from Mesopotamian texts rather than excavation. First mentioned about 3300 BCE; a tribal phase 2250-2050 BCE, then state formation on Bahrain from 2050; Kassite control in the 15th and 14th centuries; late cemeteries cautiously placed 950-700 BCE. Sargon II names King Uperi about 709 BCE, and the last mention is in a legal contract of about 510 BCE.

caveats.text: The old three-part Early, Middle and Late Dilmun scheme has been superseded by the more granular phasing above. The year of that revision is not stated in the source.

entities.summary: The Gulf trading power that stood between Mesopotamia and the Indus, and which Mesopotamian literature remembered as a kind of paradise.

entities.name: Umm an-Nar Culture
entities.date_note: Dated by tomb architecture and pottery, not radiocarbon. The start is soft: the same doctoral thesis gives 2700 BCE in one passage and 2800 in another, and other academic sources go as late as 2600.
entities.summary: The Oman peninsula's Bronze Age of circular stone tower tombs, copper export, and carnelian carried in from the Indus.

entities.name: Wadi Suq Period
entities.date_note: The 2000-1600 BC bracket was agreed in 1980 and remains the most cited. A later Bronze Age phase runs about 1600-1250 BC after it.

alternatives.label: Split into Classic and Late Wadi Suq
alternatives.note: Carter's alternative divides it at 1500 BCE and runs the later phase to 1300, which removes the need for a separate Late Bronze Age phase.

entities.summary: The southeastern Arabian second millennium, when the tower-tomb tradition breaks and burial practice changes shape.

entities.name: Saba
entities.date_note: These are LONG CHRONOLOGY dates and the choice matters. The Short Chronology, proposed by Pirenne in 1955 from art-historical and palaeographic comparison with Greece, would start South Arabian civilisation in the 5th century BCE instead — several centuries later. The one point all schemes agree on is Aelius Gallus's Roman campaign of 25 BCE. Contemporary kingdoms under the same scheme: Hadramawt and Ma'in from the 8th century, Awsan 800-500, Qataban from the 4th.

alternatives.label: Short Chronology: from the 5th century BCE
alternatives.note: Pirenne's 1955 scheme, from Greek stylistic and letter-form comparison. Not disproven, but losing ground.

caveats.text: South Arabian dates are almost never labelled with their scheme. Two sources centuries apart are usually not in conflict; they have chosen differently.

entities.summary: The incense kingdom of the Yemeni highlands, the Sheba of later legend, and the builder of the Marib Dam.

name_forms.name: Sheba
name_forms.note: The biblical form, which carried the kingdom into European tradition attached to a queen the Sabaean sources do not name.

entities.name: The Marib Dam
entities.date_note: Construction is attributed by inscription to around 700 BCE, in the era of Karib'il Watar; no scientific date confirms a construction year. The end date here is radiocarbon: AMS on detrital charcoal in the basin silts puts the dam's final period of activity no earlier than about 1 CE and no later than the end of the 3rd century. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: The famous collapse, the Sayl al-'Arim of about 570 CE, is remembered in later tradition. The sediment dating puts the dam's last activity roughly three centuries earlier.

entities.summary: Sabaean hydraulic engineering on a scale that watered a desert kingdom, and whose failure became a parable.

entities.name: The Nabataeans
entities.date_note: The first fixed reference is 312 BCE, when Diodorus records Antigonus's general attacking the Nabataean Arabs at a strong but unwalled rock, conventionally identified as Petra. The earliest Nabataean inscription naming a king, Aretas, is dated on palaeographic grounds to the first half of the 2nd century BCE and usually to 168 BCE. Rome annexed the kingdom in 106 CE.

caveats.text: Assyrian references to Nabatu and biblical Nabaioth are often taken for early Nabataeans. Most scholars now hold that none of them can be identified with the Nabataeans of Petra.

entities.summary: Caravan traders who took the northern end of the incense route, cut Petra out of sandstone, and were annexed by Rome without a fight.

entities.name: Domestication of the Dromedary
entities.date_note: Most scholars place exploitation as a pack animal no earlier than the 12th century BCE, with domestic dromedaries in southeast Arabia in the first third of the 1st millennium. In the Levant the first significant appearance is no earlier than the last third of the 10th century BCE. Wild camels are much older: bones at Baynunah in the 5th millennium and at Ra's al-Hadd at 2890-2580 BCE, neither of them domesticated.

caveats.text: Timna Site 30 was long cited for camels by the 13th century BCE. The bones belong to the site's last phase, not its Late Bronze Age layers: OxA-2165 calibrates to 969-600 BCE.
Old camel bones are not evidence of domestication. Wild dromedaries were present in Arabia for millennia before anyone rode one.

entities.summary: The pack animal that made the incense route possible, domesticated far later than the trade routes it is usually credited with opening.

entities.name: The Incense Route
entities.date_note: Conventionally described as flourishing between the 3rd century BCE and the 2nd century CE, but the route is argued to have been in use since at least the 7th century BCE and possibly the 8th. A radiocarbon date from Hajar bin Humeid of about 852 BCE with a +/-160 year error supports early South Arabian urban development, though the range is too wide to pin the trade to. Re-filed from `period` to `network`: the earlier kind misdescribed what this is.
entities.summary: Frankincense and myrrh moving north out of South Arabia, the trade that paid for Saba, Qataban and eventually Petra.

entities.name: Badarian Culture
entities.date_note: Bayesian radiocarbon gives a start of 4407-4308 and an end of 3800-3667 BCE at 68% probability, with a modelled duration of 529-709 years.

caveats.text: The Badarian ended in the 38th century BC, two to three hundred years later than typological estimates had it. Ranges like 4800-4200 BC still circulate on museum material.

entities.summary: The earliest well-defined farming culture of Upper Egypt, and the first casualty of the 2013 radiocarbon model.

entities.name: Naqada I
entities.date_note: Petrie's Sequence Dating placed this at SD 31-37, which is a relative seriation and not a calendar at all. Bayesian radiocarbon pins the Naqada IB/IC transition to 3690-3605 BCE, centuries later than typological estimates.

caveats.text: Round figures like 4000-3500 BC are conversions of a relative seriation, not measurements. They are still printed on museum education material.

entities.summary: The first phase of the Naqada sequence: black-topped pottery, white cross-lined ware, and the beginnings of a distinctly Upper Egyptian world.

entities.name: Naqada II
entities.date_note: The IID/IIIA transition is modelled at 3352-3297 BCE. The interval spanning the visible assimilation of Upper and Lower Egyptian funerary practice lasted about five or six generations.
entities.summary: Trade networks widen, burials grow unequal, and Upper Egyptian material culture starts moving north into the Delta.

entities.name: Naqada III
entities.date_note: Ends with the modelled accession of Aha at 3111-3045 BCE, median 3085. Before this model, published estimates for the foundation of the Egyptian state ranged across 3400-2900 BCE.

caveats.text: Even radiocarbon programmes disagree. The Abydos excavators' own First Dynasty dates came out 100-150 years earlier than the king-list chronology, while staying internally consistent.

entities.summary: State formation proper: walled towns, royal-scale tombs, the first writing, and the kings who came before the First Dynasty.

entities.name: The Speed of Egyptian State Formation
entities.date_note: From a Bayesian model over 186 radiocarbon dates. The paper's conclusion is comparative rather than merely chronological: prehistoric societies in Africa and Asia followed very different trajectories to political centralisation, and Egypt's was extraordinarily quick.

caveats.text: The contrast is with Southwest Asia measured the same way, from cereal agriculture to state. Egypt started farming much later, so it is the pace that differs, not the finish line.

entities.summary: Egypt went from pre-state to unified state in six or seven centuries, where the same journey in Southwest Asia took four or five millennia.

entities.name: Hierakonpolis
entities.date_note: The HK6 elite cemetery runs from about Naqada IIA through Naqada IIIC1. Dating is by Naqada-phase placement rather than radiocarbon, so sub-century precision for individual tombs should not be trusted.

caveats.text: Predynastic Egypt is often told as one centre rising. Hierakonpolis, Abydos and Naqada were competing or complementary centres, not a single seat of authority.

entities.summary: An Upper Egyptian power centre with monumental elite tombs, industrial-scale brewing, and buried elephants.

entities.name: Tomb U-j at Abydos
entities.date_note: Radiocarbon on wood from the tomb: Hd-12953 at 4470+/-30 BP calibrating to 3310-3230, 3180-3160 and 3120-3030 cal BC; Hd-12954 at 4595+/-25 BP giving 3490-3470 and 3380-3330 cal BC. Related Naqada IIIa2 tombs cluster around 3510-3100 cal BC.

caveats.text: Whether Egyptian writing was invented independently or prompted by contact with Mesopotamia is not settled. The dates are close enough that neither priority nor influence can be demonstrated.

entities.summary: The richest tomb at Abydos before the First Dynasty, holding the earliest known Egyptian writing.

entities.name: Dynasty 0
entities.date_note: A modern historiographic label, not an Egyptian one, correlated with Naqada IIIB. The succession Iry-Hor, then Ka, then Narmer may include overlapping reigns.

caveats.text: Dynasty 0 and Dynasty 00 are not standardised. Scholars draw the boundaries differently, and the order of the earliest rulers, known mainly from serekhs on pots, is not secure.

entities.summary: The rulers before the First Dynasty — Iry-Hor, Ka, Narmer — and the best argument that unification was a process rather than a moment.

entities.name: The Narmer Palette
entities.date_note: Placed at Naqada IIIC1, about 3100 BC, on typological grounds.

alternatives.label: Records an actual conquest of the Delta
alternatives.note: The historical-event reading, associated with Yurco. Long treated as conclusive evidence for military unification under Narmer.

caveats.text: It does not date a unification or show one happened as an event. It shows a smiting-and-dual-crown kingship ideology existed by about 3100 BC.
Tell el-Farkha shows no invasion layer in the Delta, and Lower Egyptian material culture had already been absorbed gradually, centuries earlier.

entities.summary: A carved schist palette showing a king smiting an enemy, and probably the most over-read object in Egyptology.

entities.name: Merimde Beni Salama
entities.date_note: Published ranges include 5300-4200, 4900-4000, 4880-4250 and 4750-4250 BC across different research groups and sample series. The wide range here is deliberate: no tighter figure is defensible. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: One of the largest Neolithic settlements of the Delta, and a site whose published dates disagree by five hundred years.

entities.name: El-Omari
entities.date_note: Published radiocarbon places it at the end of the northern Early Neolithic sequence, between 4600 and 4400 cal BC, with some sources extending to 4300. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A Lower Egyptian Neolithic settlement near Helwan, plainer in its material culture than its Upper Egyptian contemporaries.

entities.name: Maadi-Buto Culture
entities.date_note: Radiocarbon places the culture at roughly 3900-3300/3200 BC, with Buto I about 3900-3800 and the Maadi phase about 3800-3600. The transitional layer in which Naqada material replaces it falls about 3300-3200 BC.

caveats.text: This replacement is often told as the unification, coincident with Narmer. The excavated dates put it centuries earlier and show it happening gradually.

entities.summary: The last independent culture of Lower Egypt, absorbed into the expanding Naqada world well before any king unified anything.

entities.name: The Muge Shell Middens
entities.date_note: Mesolithic central Portugal is generally dated 8,500-7,000 cal BP. Deposition at Cabeco da Amoreira specifically runs 8,000-7,350 cal BP, and the first burial at Vale de Romeiras in the Sado dates to 8,543-8,334 cal BP.

caveats.text: Not a last stand before farming. The Muge and Sado foragers overlap in time with incoming Neolithic groups and interact with them for centuries.

entities.summary: Enormous mounds of estuarine shell in the Tagus and Sado valleys, used as both settlement and cemetery by foragers who overlapped with the first farmers.

entities.name: The Obanian
entities.date_note: Bulk charcoal from five Oronsay middens gave 6,200-5,400 BP uncalibrated, calibrating to about 5,150-4,250 cal BC. Bulk charcoal samples average material of different ages, so these are coarser than single-entity dates.
entities.summary: Shell middens around Oban and on Oronsay, Scotland's main evidence that late foragers there lived substantially off the sea.

entities.name: The 8.2 Kiloyear Event
entities.date_note: Dated in the NGRIP Greenland ice core by layer counting to 8,250-8,090 cal BP, which is far more precise than any of the archaeological responses being matched to it.

alternatives.label: No causal link in the Scheldt basin
alternatives.note: A multi-proxy Belgian study found little evidence connecting the 9.3 and 8.2 ka coolings to changes in human behaviour there.

caveats.text: Not a uniform catastrophe. Western Scotland shows demographic collapse, while Atlantic Iberia shows intensified shellfish use and population growth in the same window.

entities.summary: An abrupt cooling that hit Mesolithic Europe unevenly — collapse in Scotland, apparent resilience in Belgium, and growth on the Atlantic coast.

entities.name: The British Empire
entities.date_note: Neither end is a fact. The span given is the widest defensible one: Gilbert's Newfoundland claim to the Hong Kong handover, after which Britain held no significant overseas territory for the first time since 1707. Activity before the Acts of Union in 1707 was English, not British.

alternatives.label: Start 1497 (Cabot's voyage)
alternatives.note: Dates the empire from England's first overseas claim rather than any settlement.

alternatives.label: Start 1607 (Jamestown)
alternatives.note: Dates it from the first permanent settlement, the most commonly cited criterion.

alternatives.label: End 1947 (Indian independence)
alternatives.note: The most common institutional marker for the end of the imperial core.

alternatives.label: End 1956 (Suez)
alternatives.note: Diplomatic historians treat Suez as the moment imperial power was publicly exposed as spent.

caveats.text: The start is a definitional fork, not a dispute about evidence. Nobody disagrees about what happened in 1497, 1583 or 1607, only about which one counts as a beginning.
The split into a First and Second Empire hinging on 1783 is standard in tertiary sources but contested by specialists, who argue the two overlapped and the break is artificial.

entities.summary: The largest empire in history by area, and an entity whose beginning and end are both matters of definition rather than record.

entities.name: The Acts of Union
entities.date_note: Ratified 1 May 1707.
entities.summary: England and Scotland became one state, which is the point at which an English empire can properly be called British.

entities.name: Cahokia
entities.date_note: First occupied around 700 CE, with the florescence conventionally placed between about 950 and 1350.
entities.summary: The largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, and the reason 'Mississippian' names a civilization rather than a pottery style.

entities.name: Chaco Canyon
entities.date_note: Chaco's great houses are dated by tree rings, often to the year and sometimes to the felling season -- among the most precisely dated architecture anywhere before written records.
entities.summary: The administrative and ceremonial centre of the Ancestral Puebloan world, linked by engineered roads across the San Juan Basin.

entities.name: Tenochtitlan
entities.date_note: 1325 is the traditional founding date. The city fell on 13 August 1521. It predates the Triple Alliance by a century: the capital is older than the empire it came to head. Re-filed from `period` to `city`: the earlier kind misdescribed what this is.

caveats.text: 1325 is a traditional date from Mexica accounts, not an archaeological one.

entities.summary: The island capital of the Mexica, and one of the largest cities in the world when Cortés reached it.

entities.name: Monte Albán
entities.date_note: Rose to regional prominence around 500 BCE with its Classic floruit between about 300 and 900 CE.
entities.summary: The Zapotec capital on a levelled mountaintop above the Oaxaca valley.

entities.name: Tikal
entities.summary: The largest excavated Classic Maya city, and the clearest single illustration that the Maya were never one empire.

entities.name: Machu Picchu
entities.date_note: Construction is conventionally placed around 1450, in Pachacuti's reign. The site outlasts the empire: it is tied to Vilcabamba, which held out until 1572. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: A royal estate on the Vilcabamba ridge, built under Pachacuti and abandoned within a century of Spanish arrival.

entities.name: Qhapaq Ñan
entities.date_note: Built largely under the empire but incorporating far older routes, which is why the inscribed network is described as a cultural route rather than an Inca invention.
entities.summary: The Andean road network that made the empire governable, running some 30,000 kilometres across six modern countries.

entities.name: The Netherlands
entities.summary: The Dutch Republic and its successors, and the two chartered companies through which a small state ran a global trading empire.
entities.date_note: Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

entities.name: Dutch East India Company
entities.date_note: Chartered 20 March 1602; the charter lapsed on 31 December 1799. The 1798, 1799 and 1800 dates in circulation are not rival claims but three steps: the Batavian Republic assumed the company's debts in March 1798, the charter lapsed at the end of 1799, and the state took administrative control in 1800.

caveats.text: Not a company in the modern sense. Its charter granted powers of war, treaty-making, coinage and colonial government.

entities.summary: A chartered company with the power to wage war, coin money and hold territory, which for two centuries was the Dutch presence in Asia.

entities.name: Dutch West India Company
entities.date_note: Chartered 3 June 1621 and declared bankrupt by the States General in September 1674. This is the first company; a second followed immediately under a near-identical charter, and sources that give '1621-1794' have run the two together.
entities.summary: The Atlantic counterpart of the VOC: Brazil, the Caribbean, New Netherland, and a dominant share of the Dutch slave trade.

entities.name: Second Dutch West India Company
entities.date_note: Chartered 1675 and wound up on 1 January 1792, having been abolished by decision in 1791.

alternatives.label: Ends 1791 (abolition decided)
alternatives.note: The States General decided not to renew the patent in 1791; the formal end followed on 1 January 1792.

alternatives.label: Ends 1794 (French invasion)
alternatives.note: Britannica dates the dissolution to the French invasion of the Dutch Republic.

entities.summary: The successor company, narrower in remit and increasingly dependent on the slave trade.

entities.name: First French Colonial Empire
entities.date_note: Both ends are choices. 1534 is Cartier's claim rather than a settlement, and the end depends on which loss counts as terminal.

alternatives.label: 1605-1803 (Port Royal to the Louisiana sale)
alternatives.note: Dates the empire from the first actual colony and ends it with the sale of Louisiana rather than the Napoleonic collapse.

entities.summary: New France, the Caribbean sugar islands and the Indian trading posts, most of it lost or sold within two generations.

entities.name: Second French Colonial Empire
entities.date_note: 1830 is the invasion of Algiers and is essentially uncontested. The end is Algerian independence, declared on 5 July 1962 -- a date chosen to fall exactly 132 years after the landing, which makes it a commemorative convention as much as an administrative fact.

caveats.text: 5 July 1962 is a symbolic date. The Evian ceasefire was in March and France recognised independence on 3 July.

entities.summary: Rebuilt around Algeria and expanded across West and Central Africa and Indochina, and dismantled in fifteen years after 1945.

entities.name: The Georgian Era
entities.date_note: 1714 is George I's accession on the death of Queen Anne. The end is disputed: 1830 with George IV, the last of the four Georges, or 1837 with William IV, which is the boundary with the Victorian era.

name_forms.name: Regency era
name_forms.note: Strictly the regency of George IV as Prince of Wales during his father's illness, though used loosely for the wider period.

alternatives.label: Ends 1830 (death of George IV)
alternatives.note: Ends the era with the last of the four kings it is named after.

entities.name: Multi-Regional Empires
entities.date_note: The span runs from the Achaemenids to the Hong Kong handover and is a container rather than a claim. Each empire here is also reachable from every region it held, so a reader browsing Anatolia or the Nile finds the Ottomans without coming here first. Grouping the caliphates, the Mongols and the European maritime empires for comparison is a deliberate scholarly move: Burbank and Cooper treat them as comparable, and the Oxford World History of Empire frames the comparison as a corrective to older single-region imperial history. entities.name: Namazga Sequence
entities.date_note: RECEIVED FRAMEWORK, NOT A DATED ONE. The phases in general circulation are Namazga I 4800-4000, II 4000-3500, III 3500-3000, IV 3000-2500, V 2500-2200 and VI 2200-1500 BCE, and competing bracket sets exist for most of them. They descend from Masson's Soviet-era ceramic typology; no published radiocarbon table for Namazga-depe itself supports them. Where independent dating does exist it disagrees: modern reassessments compress the Namazga V urban phase into roughly 2400-1950 or 2250-1700 BCE, and one report gives C14 dates for a single final Namazga VI layer scattering from 1884 to 818 BC. Use the phase names to talk to the literature; do not use these numbers as dates.

caveats.text: These phase brackets are a typological convention, not measurements. Treating Namazga V as a dated period rather than a pottery style is the standard error.

entities.summary: The six-phase framework that every account of Central Asian prehistory is written in, and which rests on pottery typology rather than radiocarbon.

entities.name: Kelteminar Culture
entities.date_note: A peer-reviewed source places Kelteminar in the sixth to fourth millennia BC in general terms, and that is the whole of the defensible dating. No site-level radiocarbon dataset with lab numbers was locatable for any Kelteminar site, and the field disagrees about the culture's geographic and temporal boundaries — the authors of that paper decline to label their own 9200-7800 cal BP material at Toda-1 Cave as Kelteminar for that reason.
entities.summary: Hunter-fisher-gatherers of the Aral basin and the Amu Darya delta, in contact with the farming villages to their south.

entities.name: Altyn-Depe
entities.date_note: Dated by its Namazga V pottery, so it inherits that sequence's problem entirely. The excavator's own figures — Early Namazga V c. 2100-1850 BC, Late c. 1850-1650 — are typological. No modern radiocarbon programme for the site was locatable, so nothing here is independent of the ceramic framework.
entities.summary: A walled town of the Namazga culture with a stepped tower, craft quarters and trade reaching Mundigak and Shahr-i Sokhta.

entities.name: Epipalaeolithic (Levant)
entities.date_note: Calibrated to IntCal20. Its end at 10,000 BC is exactly where 'Mesolithic (Eurasia)' starts, and that is the point: the two are largely the same idea under different regional naming traditions, not adjacent periods. This entry exists because the EARLY part, back to 23,000 BC, sits inside the Palaeolithic band where nothing else names it. Absolute figures vary by several centuries across calibration vintages. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: Not a separate stage from the Mesolithic: the Near East, North Africa and southern Europe say Epipalaeolithic where northern Europe says Mesolithic.

entities.summary: The long Levantine hunter-gatherer sequence between the Upper Palaeolithic and farming, ending where the Mesolithic begins.

entities.name: Kebaran
entities.date_note: The Oxford IntCal20 table gives 23,000-16,000 cal BC for the Early Epipalaeolithic as a whole. Kebaran-only figures differ across sources (c. 18,000-14,500 BP on the coast), and no single end date is settled. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The Early Epipalaeolithic of the Levant: small mobile groups with microlithic toolkits, through the Last Glacial Maximum.

entities.name: Geometric Kebaran
entities.date_note: 16,000-13,000 cal BC, IntCal20. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The Middle Epipalaeolithic, named for its geometric microliths, between the Kebaran and the Natufian.

entities.name: Chalcolithic (Southeast Europe)
entities.date_note: Copper minerals are worked from c. 6200 BC and native copper from c. 5500 BC, but the Chalcolithic proper begins with smelting at c. 5000 BC. Belovode in Serbia holds the earliest securely dated smelting anywhere, and specialists expect that status to move. There is no global Chalcolithic node, deliberately. Most of sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron; China folds early copper into the Late Neolithic; the Americas never reached a continent-wide Bronze Age; and Australian archaeology has dropped three-age terminology altogether. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: A Copper Age is not a universal stage. Most of sub-Saharan Africa has none at all, moving from stone tools directly to iron.

entities.summary: The Balkan Copper Age: the world's earliest known copper smelting, and the gold of the Varna cemetery.

entities.name: Chalcolithic (Southern Levant)
entities.date_note: c. 4700/4500-3700/3600 cal BC is the most consistently defended range; some syntheses broaden it to 5000-3500 BC. Both internal boundaries are described in the literature as imprecisely dated, and whether the Chalcolithic overlaps Early Bronze I is disputed. There is no global Chalcolithic node, deliberately. Most of sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron; China folds early copper into the Late Neolithic; the Americas never reached a continent-wide Bronze Age; and Australian archaeology has dropped three-age terminology altogether. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The southern Levantine Copper Age, with copper hoards, ossuary burial and the Ghassulian culture.

entities.name: Chalcolithic (Anatolia)
entities.date_note: c. 5500-3000 BC is the most commonly defended whole-period range, but at least three incompatible sub-periodizations are in active use for Central, Eastern and Western Anatolia, differing by centuries. Treat any single Anatolian figure with caution. There is no global Chalcolithic node, deliberately. Most of sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron; China folds early copper into the Late Neolithic; the Americas never reached a continent-wide Bronze Age; and Australian archaeology has dropped three-age terminology altogether. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: The Anatolian Copper Age, spanning the long interval between the Neolithic villages and the Early Bronze Age.

entities.name: Late Chalcolithic (Mesopotamia)
entities.date_note: In Mesopotamian usage 'Chalcolithic' covers the pre-Bronze sequence, and the narrower Late Chalcolithic runs c. 4500-3100 BC. Note this ends 200 years AFTER the global Bronze Age node begins at 3300 BC: the regional Bronze Age does not start until Uruk closes. There is no global Chalcolithic node, deliberately. Most of sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron; China folds early copper into the Late Neolithic; the Americas never reached a continent-wide Bronze Age; and Australian archaeology has dropped three-age terminology altogether. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: Terminal Ubaid through Late Uruk, the LC1-LC5 sequence that ends with the first cities and the first writing.

entities.name: Chalcolithic (South Asia)
entities.date_note: No single pan-Indian range is defensible. These cultures run c. 3000/2600 BC to c. 700 BC and are CONTEMPORARY with, not prior to, mature Harappan Bronze Age urbanism elsewhere in the subcontinent — which is why no global Chalcolithic node can exist. Jorwe alone runs to c. 700 BC, inside the global Iron Age band. There is no global Chalcolithic node, deliberately. Most of sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron; China folds early copper into the Late Neolithic; the Americas never reached a continent-wide Bronze Age; and Australian archaeology has dropped three-age terminology altogether. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

caveats.text: Not the stage between Neolithic and Bronze Age here: South Asian Chalcolithic cultures coexist with Bronze Age cities nearby.

entities.summary: The Deccan and central Indian copper-using farming cultures — Kayatha, Ahar-Banas, Malwa and Jorwe — which are not a pre-Bronze stage at all.

Jomon's primary home stays under Japan, because it is Japan's founding era rather than a detachable prehistoric episode.
